summary.text: Abstract algebra is the study of algebraic structures, which are sets with specific operations acting on their elements.
Algebraic structures include groups, rings, fields, modules, vector spaces, lattices and algebras over a field.
It grew during the nineteenth century from scattered facts in several branches of mathematics and was unified in the early 20th century into formal definitions.

facts.label: Name coined
facts.value: In the early 20th century, to set it apart from elementary algebra

facts.label: Before the 1800s
facts.value: Algebra was defined as the study of polynomials

facts.label: Unification
facts.value: Early 20th century formal definitions of groups, rings and fields

facts.label: Today's usage
facts.value: Simply called algebra; the longer name is mostly used in teaching

facts.label: Inverse requirement
facts.value: Von Dyck in 1882 first required inverse elements in a group

items.prompt: A mathematician takes a set together with a rule for combining its elements and studies that pair as an object in itself. What is such a thing called in abstract algebra?
items.explain: Abstract algebra studies algebraic structures, which are sets with specific operations acting on their elements.

items.prompt: The name abstract algebra was coined to set it apart from an older kind of algebra. What does that older kind do?

options.label: Uses variables to stand for numbers in computation
Studies only sets with one operation
Avoids all symbols and uses words

items.explain: Elementary algebra is the use of variables to represent numbers in computation and reasoning.

items.prompt: A textbook opens each chapter with a formal definition of a structure and then gives examples. Is that how the subject developed historically?

options.label: Yes, definitions came first and examples followed
Nearly the opposite: concrete problems came first
No, because examples were never used

items.explain: Theories started as scattered facts from concrete problems and were unified into formal definitions only in the early 20th century.

items.prompt: In 1854 Cayley defined a group as a set with an associative operation and an identity, without asking for inverses. What is that called today?
items.explain: That definition describes what is today called a monoid; inverses were first required later.

items.prompt: What marks Peacock's symbolical algebra as different from the older arithmetical algebra?

options.label: Its rules of operation hold with no restrictions
It was written entirely in words
It required one number to exceed another

items.explain: In arithmetical algebra a − b is restricted to a ≥ b, while in symbolical algebra all rules hold with no restrictions.

items.prompt: In 1832 the word group was first used for a certain collection of permutations. What property of the collection did it signify?

options.label: It could be written in words only

items.explain: Galois used the term for a collection of permutations closed under composition.
